And they created some- thing grand that expanded pretty far and put a lot of people on the map locally, regionally and nationally.” I know that I did make the right deci- sion to move to Nashville,” she added. “But I want this to be a situation where I’m able to go back and forth because I denitely miss Charleston a lot.” IF YOU WANT TO GO: Doors open at 5 p.m. Nov. 19, Charleston Pour House, 1977 Maybank Highway, Charleston. Tickets range from $15 to $20: charlestonpourhouse.com The education focus was always the plan for the 2015 reopening of the center. “We wanted to become the commu- nity’s largest classroom … where the community not only had a grand space where they could be a part of the arts, but a space where everyone felt welcome,” said deVries. How the Gaillard diers from performing arts centers across the United States is to select content based on how it connects to South Carolina’s academic standards. “Every performance we bring comple- ments the state standards, supports the class, the classroom curriculum that the teachers are already teaching, so that the students can master those state academic standards, but also give them a lens and a clear view of the world of the arts and the endless possibilities of the arts,” she said. At the Gaillard, it’s not just a single prong of a show that supports the cur- riculum, deVries noted, but also a show where every child has an opportunity throughout the season to see someone that looks like them on their stage and be inspired knowing that they too can explore the world of the arts. The Gibbes gains ground Then there is the Gibbes Museum of Art, which has been committed to arts educa- tion since its founding as the Carolina Art Association in 1858. “Our intention from the start has been to educate through art, the creation of art, and access to art,” President and CEO Alex Rich told the Charleston City P ap e r . “From our beginnings, and espe- cially once we moved into our present building and rst permanent site in 1905, we have explored both the history of art and the processes underlying the production of art.” Soon the museum will have a new space to further this mission. A dedicated Center for Education is set to open in April in the former oces for South Carolina Electric and Gas (and then Dominion Energy) at 141 Meeting St. It’s a game-changer for the Gibbes’s commitment to education to accommodate a broadened array of oerings, from early childhood learning to senior education. With its separate entrance directly o of Meeting Street, it allows for easy access for school buses and tour groups. “We want to break down barriers to learning in the space of the museum, addressing audiences of all abilities no matter how they interact with us,” said Rich. The current programming extends to learners of all ages, with particular stand- outs in its sold-out summer camps as well as new oerings like Tiny Tours, Drawn Together and First Look for Kids. General audiences can immerse themselves in pro- grams including its lecture series, hands- on artmaking workshops and open-hours with visiting artists. Last year, the Scrollathon initiative oered an opportunity to nearly 300 members of the community to contribute to a collective artwork made up of indi- vidually fabric scrolls, all inspired by the theme of America’s 250th, with the Gibbes representing South Carolina. “That was perhaps the most joyful week I have witnessed personally in my time at the Gibbes, alongside the opening reception for our recent collaboration with HEART inclusive art community on an exhibition called Taking Up Space and featuring the work of artists with disabili- ties,” Rich said, demonstrating that the joy of learning has much to teach us all.
